anchors.quote: For each elimination column, define a finite search over row indices i in [col,n). Mark exactly the first index whose absolute pivot value is maximal: P(i) holds when no candidate row has a larger abs(rows[k][col]) and no earlier candidate row has an equal value. A Grover-style subroutine could conditionally search for this unique marked index. The surrounding classical loop, exact-zero check, row swap, elimination, back substitution, overflow checks, and reporting remain unchanged.

Encode candidate row indices in a register and provide coherent read access to the current binary64 rows and column index. A reversible predicate must compare abs(rows[i][col]) against every eligible row, implement the first-index tie rule, handle the non-power-of-two index range, and uncompute all comparison workspace. The representation and reversible implementation of Python binary64 absolute values and comparisons, including signed zero behavior, remain unresolved.

Measure a row index, reject out-of-range results, and classically verify that it is the first index attaining the largest absolute pivot value. If verification fails or the quantum procedure does not return a verified index, use the original classical max operation. After verification, preserve the exact-zero singularity check and deterministic row swap.
Finite development checks would not prove full-domain equivalence for all validated binary64 inputs or evolving elimination states.
